claims.text: Advanced free-energy sampling can guide processing conditions for NM-HEAs.
Free-energy-sampling-guided processing will facilitate self-assembly of a three-dimensional NM-HEA nanoframework.
Atomic-scale nucleation and selective-dealloying pathways can be accurately tuned through this approach.
The precursor NM-HEA has a homogeneously mixed elemental composition.
The precursor is produced by conventional alloying and initially lacks a defined nanoframework architecture.
Atomistic simulations can investigate atomic-scale structural and chemical evolution in a noble-metal-containing high-entropy nanoalloy.
Free-energy sampling coupled with atomistic simulation can map nucleation, growth, and dealloying pathways.
Simulation can identify optimal temperature, electrochemical potential, and selective-dissolution parameters for nanoframework synthesis.
A simulation-tailored free-energy landscape will favor interconnected porous structures under selective-dealloying conditions.
Atomic nucleation-site distributions and dealloying fronts govern nanoframework self-assembly and interconnectivity.
Mapping the free-energy landscape permits stabilization of intermediate phases and governs selective dealloying.
Controlled nucleation and dealloying direct precise atomic rearrangements toward a uniformly alloyed, interconnected three-dimensional nanoframework.
Free-energy-sampling-guided synthesis will produce a porous NM-HEA nanoframework with greater connectivity and a uniform elemental distribution.
High-resolution microscopy can resolve atomic-scale structural evolution in NM-HEA nanoparticles.
Conventional bulk melting followed by non-directed dealloying yields irregular morphologies, phase segregation, or non-uniform nanoarchitectures.
Failure to reproduce the simulated free-energy landscape or the presence of kinetic barriers may prevent formation of the expected equilibrium nanoframework.
The proposed mechanism is supported by simulation-guided parameter optimization.
The magnitude and reproducibility of structural improvement remain uncertain because of experimental variability and sensitivity to processing parameters.
